opinions.rationale: Inverted-prior search for regulatory acceptance thresholds on emulation adequacy, residual confounding, or sufficient sensitivity analysis did not find any. The problem’s own cited instruments still describe process and design expectations without numeric or decision-rule cutoffs. FDA July 2024 final guidance on EHR and claims data (and related non-interventional RWE guidance) recommends quantitative bias analysis for misclassification and reliability issues, fitness-for-use assessment, and transparent causal design including target trial emulation where appropriate, but does not state how close an emulation must be, how large residual confounding may be, or which sensitivity package is enough for acceptance. NICE’s RWE framework explicitly treats some target trials as not adequately emulable and prefers bespoke collection in those cases; secondary commentary on the final framework notes that NICE deliberately does not set minimum acceptable quality standards. EMA’s March 2025 reflection paper on RWD in non-interventional studies for regulatory purposes (EMA/99865/2025) endorses target trial emulation for causal objectives, ICH E9(R1)-aligned sensitivity analysis, and case-by-case relevance determination; it does not supply thresholds. ICH E9(R1) remains a trial estimand and sensitivity framework, not a translation into emulation acceptance rules. Adjacent methods work (E-values, tipping-point and quantitative bias analysis, Faries et al. 2025 good practices for robustness of observational evidence) equip sponsors to quantify bias under assumed parameters; that is not a regulator-issued decision threshold, and any fixed numeric bar would still be decision-dependent as the report states. No 2024–2026 FDA, EMA, HMA, ICH, NICE, Health Canada, CDA-AMC, or ENCePP instrument located here closes the gap. Queries included: FDA/NICE/EMA residual confounding threshold and acceptance criteria; quantitative bias analysis regulatory threshold; ICH E9(R1) observational thresholds; ENCePP/DARWIN acceptance criteria 2025–2026; plus review of the three cited guidance PDFs and the 2025 EMA reflection paper.

No adopted, author-facing assumption dashboard that separates diagnosable diagnostics from undiagnosable identifying assumptions for target trial emulations was found. TARGET (Hansford/Cashin et al., JAMA 2025; also BMJ co-publication) is a 21-item reporting guideline for observational studies that explicitly emulate a target trial: it requires statement of the target protocol, mapping to data, identifying assumptions, and sensitivity analyses. It is deliberately not a risk-of-bias tool and not a standardized diagnostic panel; its own positioning matches the report’s prior-work note. Hansford et al. JAMA Netw Open 2023 documents uneven reporting of emulation components, which is baseline practice, not a dashboard. ROBINS-I and ROBINS-I V2 (launch materials 2024) structure reviewer risk-of-bias judgments relative to a specified target trial; that is systematic-review assessment, not a publication convention that forces authors to display balance over time, weight tails, effective sample size, support by treatment history, phenotype validity, and sensitivity contours in a fixed layout with testable panels visually separated from exchangeability and consistency. STaRT-RWE and HARPER improve protocol prespecification and reproducibility; they do not standardize longitudinal diagnostic summaries. Software ecosystems (cobalt, WeightIt, MatchIt, ipw, gfoRmula, lmtp, ltmle, adjustedCurves) supply balance, overlap, and weight diagnostics for specific designs, including some longitudinal use, but there is no field-wide agreed summary statistic for longitudinal balance or support-by-history, and no journal or regulator-mandated dashboard that makes omission of a panel a visible reporting failure. Method papers that propose or apply QBA, negative controls, or multi-panel diagnostics remain proposals or local practice, not an adopting-body convention. The core structural claim remains: conventions require adoption, and none has closed the reported gap. Queries included: assumption/diagnostic dashboard target trial; TARGET as diagnostic standard; longitudinal balance standardization cobalt WeightIt; ROBINS-I TTE diagnostics; STaRT-RWE HARPER assumption reporting 2024–2026; arXiv/medRxiv causal diagnostic checklist.

The claim is that the label target trial emulation is used as a credibility credential rather than as a design description of temporal alignment and protocol specification, and that no shared vocabulary states which step on an assumption-to-conclusion ladder a study reaches. Literature search under the inverted prior found restatements and measurements of this problem, not a solved convention. Hubbard and Hernán (N Engl J Med 2024) state what emulation does and does not secure, call sensitivity analysis for unobserved confounding essential, and explicitly deny that the framework is a panacea; that strengthens the conceptual distinction the problem describes and does not install a journal-level rung vocabulary or stop label-as-credibility use. Hansford et al. JAMA Netw Open 2023 quantifies weak adherence among studies that claim to emulate a trial (large fractions missing key components or dual protocol/emulation description), which shows the label does not bind practice. TARGET (2025) improves transparent reporting of the emulation claim and assumptions but does not replace the label with a required statement of the highest justified causal step, nor invent named intermediate rungs from association through measured confounding, sustained strategies, and transport. No 2024–2026 journal policy or reporting addendum was found that requires authors to declare an assumption ladder rung instead of (or in addition to) the TTE label, and no widely adopted named vocabulary for intermediate rungs was located. Commentaries that warn against over-reading TTE as causal certification reinforce that the misuse remains live. Proposal-stage ladders outside TTE (generic credibility ladders in other fields) do not solve the emulation-label problem as stated. Queries included: TTE label overused credibility; assumption ladder target trial; journal policy require emulation components 2024–2026; Hubbard Hernán potential pitfalls follow-on; TARGET vs causal claim strength.
